clue.text: Attractive secretary and PA put it differently

indicators.note: saying something differently means rearranging it, so the letters before are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; these words do double duty in the indicator

explanation.surface: Someone tactfully rephrases a remark about an office secretary and a personal assistant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put it' is both part of the fodder and part of the phrase 'put it differently'; all sixteen letters of secretary, PA and put it rearrange to PRETTY AS A PICTURE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone very good-looking, so it can stand for the adjective meaning appealing to the eye.

clue.text: Persuasive leader spotted parking in wharf

indicators.note: one thing placed in another, so the abbreviation goes inside the word for a landing stage

blocks.note: pied means patchy in colour, like a magpie
a landing stage jutting into water
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A spotted car parked on a wharf, cast as a persuasive leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as seen, but it means patchy-coloured, as in a piebald horse.
explanation.definitionFit: In the folk tale the piper of Hamelin lured rats and then children away, so the name now means anyone who persuades followers.

clue.text: Enigmatic composer perhaps left in temper when rebuffed

indicators.note: one letter is placed in the word for anger
a rebuff turns something back, so in a down clue the letters are read upwards

blocks.note: rage is a fit of temper
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A mysterious composer, rebuffed, is left in a bad temper.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes into RAGE, making RAGLE, which reads backwards as the answer. Edward Elgar wrote the Enigma Variations, hence 'Enigmatic composer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elgar's best-known orchestral work is the Enigma Variations, so he is an example of a composer linked with enigma.

clue.text: This would be very windy road not repaired

indicators.note: something not repaired is still broken, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A road left unrepaired after a violent storm would be twisting and windy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a broken-up road is just what such a storm leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent rotating storm, about as windy as weather gets.

clue.text: Three articles about Northern Ireland — in Greek

indicators.note: about means around, so the articles surround the abbreviation

blocks.note: the articles a, the and an
NI is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Three articles are written about Northern Ireland, in the Greek language.
explanation.walkthrough: The articles are the grammatical kind, the indefinite pair and the definite one, not newspaper pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An Athenian is a native of Athens, the Greek capital, so the word is one kind of Greek.

clue.text: British sport fitting screens without warning

indicators.note: a screen surrounds and hides something, so one word wraps the others

blocks.note: apt means suitable
B is the abbreviation for British
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A fitting British sport shown on screens without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: APT wraps B plus RU, the usual shorthand for rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrupt means sudden, happening with no notice beforehand.

clue.text: Wife up with latest trends becomes party disciplinarian

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
hip means fashionable

explanation.surface: A fashionable wife ends up enforcing order in a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: A party whip is the MP who keeps colleagues voting along party lines in the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: In Parliament a whip is the official who enforces party discipline at votes.

clue.text: Commoners vote amid hard calls for attention?

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one word sits inside the others

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
oi is a shout to get attention, so two of them
a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: A vote held amid loud calls for attention.
explanation.walkthrough: Oi is the informal British shout used to catch someone's attention; H for hard comes from pencil grades.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek for 'the many', the phrase is used in English for the common people or masses.

clue.text: Creature devours rook and crustacean

indicators.note: something devoured ends up inside the eater, so one word takes in a letter

blocks.note: a creature in the sense of someone used as a tool by another
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: A creature eats a rook and a shellfish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creature' reads as an animal but means a puppet or pawn; R goes inside to make PRAWN.
explanation.definitionFit: A prawn is a small edible shellfish, one of the crustaceans.

clue.text: Floor very very old in state

blocks.note: to floor someone is to knock them out, KO
so means very
V is the abbreviation for very
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A floor in a very, very old state of repair.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'very' is used two ways: once as SO, once as V.
explanation.definitionFit: Kosovo is a Balkan country that declared independence in 2008, so it is a state.

clue.text: Seeing bear regularly in Alpine landmark

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Spotting a bear at regular intervals on a famous Alpine peak.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eiger is a famous Swiss mountain known for its north face, a landmark of the Alps.

clue.text: Organ damage on vicar's insides

indicators.note: insides are what lies within, so the outer letters are dropped

blocks.note: harm means damage
taken as written
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Damage done to a church organ is put down to the vicar's innards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests a church instrument, matching the vicar, but the answer is a mouth organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica is commonly called a mouth organ, a small instrument played by blowing.

clue.text: Painter struggling to be relevant

indicators.note: someone struggling is thrown about, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An artist struggling to stay relevant.
explanation.definitionFit: To pertain is to relate to or concern something, which is what being relevant means.

clue.text: See 14
It is what it is

blocks.note: surface reading: the shrug of acceptance, things are as they are
setter's reading: the word 'it' is defined by its grammatical category

explanation.walkthrough: The stock phrase of resignation hides a grammar lesson: the first 'It' is the word itself, and the rest names what kind of word it is.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar 'it' belongs to the class of words like I, you and she that stand for people or things.

clue.text: Minded going under ladders? Show extreme fear!

indicators.note: in a down entry, something going under another word is placed below it

blocks.note: a ladder in tights is a run
minded means cared, as in 'I don't mind'

explanation.surface: Someone superstitious about walking under ladders is told to show their fear.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder is the British term for a run in stockings or tights; 'Minded' is the past of mind, as in 'I wouldn't mind'.
explanation.definitionFit: To run scared is an idiom for acting in panic, which is showing great fear.

clue.text: Looked to journey back then went ahead

indicators.note: going back means reading the word for travel from right to left

blocks.note: to go is to journey
led means went in front

explanation.surface: Looking to make a return trip, then going on ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looked to' reads as 'hoped to', but 'Looked' alone is the definition and 'to' runs into the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to look at someone with obvious desire, so ogled is a particular way of having looked.

clue.text: One taking the lead in spiritual band?

blocks.note: first meaning: the strap on a dog's neck that a leash clips to
second meaning: the stiff white neckband worn by clergy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking the lead' reads as leading a group, and 'band' as a group of musicians; the lead is a leash and the band is a strip round the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy's stiff white collars are nicknamed after the pet's neck strap, so the phrase covers both.

clue.text: Page with Lima in the map redrawn for publication

indicators.note: one letter is put in among the following words
a map that is redrawn is made again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for page
taken as written
Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A page showing Lima on a redrawn map, ready for publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lima' suggests the Peruvian capital on a map, but it is just the letter L from the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pamphlet is a small unbound booklet, a kind of printed publication.

clue.text: Old characters in works conserving energy

indicators.note: to conserve is to hold on to, so one word keeps a letter inside it

blocks.note: a machine that works runs
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned characters in a play, about saving energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are the letters of ancient Germanic alphabets, so they are old written characters.

clue.text: Team docked five hundred pounds? Sudden blow!

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a squad is a team
D is the Roman numeral for 500
L is the symbol for a pound, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A team fined five hundred pounds: what a blow!
explanation.walkthrough: SQUAD loses its D, then two Ls follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A squall is a sudden violent gust of wind, so it is a blow in the weather sense.

clue.text: See 28
Presumably a bottle party? That's impossible

blocks.note: a bottle is presumably not a can
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A party where you bring your own bottle is declared off.
explanation.walkthrough: A bottle party is a British gathering where each guest brings a drink; the wordplay jokes that a bottle, presumably, is no can.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is a flat refusal meaning the thing asked cannot be done.

clue.text: Compensate rabble discontented with putsch

indicators.note: without its contents the word keeps only its outer shell

blocks.note: first and last letters only
a putsch is a sudden seizure of power

explanation.surface: Discontented rabble demanding compensation after an attempted putsch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' reads as unhappy, the rabble's mood, but it means emptied of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To recoup is to make up for or recover losses, which is to compensate.

clue.text: See 1
Silence from gym guru?

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school gym
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A fitness guru calls for quiet in the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: Peace is a state of quiet or calm, as in 'peace and quiet', so it can mean silence.

clue.text: Photos thus framing a Cubist pioneer

indicators.note: a frame goes around a picture, so one word surrounds a letter

blocks.note: pics is short for pictures
taken as written
so means thus

explanation.surface: Photographs framing a pioneering Cubist painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Photos' takes the casual short form, as people say pics.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque founded Cubism, the early twentieth-century art movement.

clue.text: Lower and lower going into small lake?

indicators.note: going into something places it inside, so a word sits between two letters

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a lower is something that lows, or moos
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Something lowering further and further into a small lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word is read two ways: 'Lower' rhyming with 'hour' means to frown, and 'lower' rhyming with 'flower' is a cow that moos.
explanation.definitionFit: To lower, also spelt lour, is to look sullen or threatening, which is what a frown does.

clue.text: Occasional butt from goat chasing girl

indicators.note: a chaser comes behind what it pursues, so this word follows the other

blocks.note: April is a girl's name
a silly goat is a fool

explanation.surface: A goat butting a girl from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butt' suggests a goat's charge but means the target of a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is the victim of a prank on 1 April, so a target of jokes only once a year.

clue.text: Plain refusal from the dedicated watercolourist?

blocks.note: first meaning: unattractive in appearance
second meaning, read literally: a watercolour painter would refuse to work in oils

explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom is said of someone not good-looking; the question mark flags the jokey literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying someone is no oil painting is a British idiom for calling them homely or unattractive.

clue.text: Inspired Darwish pens literary collection

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the letters sit inside the words before

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: An inspired poet named Darwish writes a literary anthology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' reads as writes, but it means encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is a medieval Icelandic compilation of Norse myths and poems, a literary collection.

clue.text: Scribbler's book likely to be steamy?

blocks.note: first meaning: a hack writer's quickly written novel
second meaning, read literally: something that boils a pot gives off steam

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steamy' suggests a racy novel, but the second reading is a heater for pots.
explanation.definitionFit: A potboiler is a mediocre work churned out just to earn a living, or to keep the pot boiling.
